title: Admin table with bulk destructive operations

brief.job: Identify and disable obsolete third-party application connections while avoiding active production integrations.
brief.consequence: Disabling an active connection interrupts a business workflow; leaving an obsolete one active leaves unnecessary access in place.
facts: There are 46 application connections. Each record has application, owner, environment, scopes, last successful use, token expiry, and status.

Five records are shown in the initial data: SurveyShip, Lila Chen, production, contacts.read and deals.write, last used 2 days ago, expires in 78 days, active; Old CRM Export, Arun Shah, production, contacts.read, last used 418 days ago, expires in 12 days, active; Payroll Archive, Dana Cole, production, payroll.read, last used 391 days ago, expires in 31 days, active; Sandbox Sync, Lila Chen, sandbox, contacts.read, last used 201 days ago, expires in 4 days, active; Legacy Forms, no owner, production, contacts.read and forms.write, last used 502 days ago, expired, active.

An obsolete candidate is active, has no successful use in 180 days, and is not marked production-critical. Production-critical is not supplied for any initial record, so the administrator must inspect before bulk action.

Available record actions are view details, notify owner, disable, and delete. Disable is reversible by an administrator. Delete is destructive and requires a typed count confirmation. Bulk disable is allowed; bulk delete is not.
The table default should help locate stale access, but it must preserve a way to inspect usage and scope before action.

required_states: bulk-action error for one selected record
acceptance_checks: A reviewer can distinguish stale candidates from active production connections before acting.
Delete never presents as the casual bulk default.
The initial records and their uncertainty are preserved exactly.
